# Fine-Tuning LLMs: LoRA to AWS Bedrock

![](images/fine-tuning-llms.png){.post-banner fig-alt="Fine-Tuning LLMs"}

There are two practical ways to fine-tune an LLM: train a LoRA adapter yourself with Hugging Face, or hand the job to a managed service like Bedrock. This post covers the minimum you need for the first, how supervised fine-tuning compares to continued pre-training, DPO and RLHF, how to get a LoRA model into Bedrock, and then the three Bedrock customization workflows (reinforcement fine-tuning, supervised fine-tuning, distillation) with the data format, launch call and evaluation for each.

## Full Fine-Tuning vs PEFT

Full fine-tuning updates every weight in the model. It gives the most control, but it's expensive in GPU memory and easy to overfit on small datasets. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like **LoRA** ([Hu et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)) freeze the base model and train small low-rank adapter matrices instead, cutting trainable parameters to around 1% of the model while staying close to full fine-tuning quality on most instruction-tuning tasks.

```python
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model_id = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,
    lora_alpha=32,
    target_modules="all-linear",
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)

model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
```

`target_modules="all-linear"` adapts every attention and MLP projection rather than only `q_proj`/`v_proj`. See [the Llama 3 8B walkthrough](lora-finetuning-8b.qmd) for why, what `r` and `lora_alpha` actually control, and a full training loop with TRL.

### Before you train

- Keep examples in a consistent instruction/response format.
- Favor quality over quantity. A few thousand well-curated examples usually beat a large noisy dataset.
- Deduplicate aggressively; repeated examples skew the model more than expected.
- Track validation loss, but don't stop there. Run side-by-side comparisons against the base model on real prompts, because loss going down doesn't always mean the outputs are better for your task.

Start small with LoRA on a subset of the data before committing to a full fine-tune or a larger training run.

## Choosing a Training Signal: SFT, Continued Pre-Training, DPO, RLHF

LoRA answers *which weights* get updated. It says nothing about *what signal* drives the update. Everything above is supervised fine-tuning (SFT): next-token loss on labeled completions. The same LoRA adapter can just as well be trained on raw text, on preference pairs, or on a reward, and the choice of signal usually matters more than the choice between LoRA and a full fine-tune.

| Method | Training data | Objective | What it changes | Relative cost | Bedrock `customizationType` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continued pre-training | Raw, unlabeled domain text (millions to billions of tokens) | Next-token loss on every token | Vocabulary, facts, domain style | High (data volume) | `CONTINUED_PRE_TRAINING` |
| SFT | Prompt/completion pairs (hundreds to tens of thousands) | Next-token loss on completion tokens only | Output format, task behavior, tone | Low | `FINE_TUNING` |
| DPO | Prompt + chosen + rejected responses | Logistic loss on the log-prob margin vs a frozen reference | Which of several plausible answers the model prefers | Low to medium | None |
| RLHF / RL | Preference comparisons for a reward model (or a programmatic grader), then prompts | Maximize reward with a KL penalty to the starting model | Same as DPO, plus behavior on prompts outside the preference set | High | `REINFORCEMENT_FINE_TUNING` (GRPO) |

Distillation, the fourth Bedrock workflow, isn't a separate signal: it's SFT on responses generated by a larger teacher model.

### Continued pre-training

Continued pre-training (also called domain-adaptive pre-training, see [Gururangan et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.10964)) keeps running the original pre-training objective on a corpus from your domain: legal filings, clinical notes, an internal codebase. There are no prompts or labels, so the model learns the distribution of the text itself. It is the one method in this list that reliably adds *knowledge*, which matters because a low-rank SFT adapter is a weak tool for teaching new facts.

There are two catches. It needs far more data than SFT to move the needle, and it erodes general and instruction-following ability if the corpus is narrow. The usual recipe mixes some general-domain text back into the corpus, then runs a short SFT pass afterwards to restore chat behavior. Bedrock exposes it with `{"input": "..."}` records, but [only for Amazon Titan text models](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/dataset-prep-continued-pretraining.html).

### DPO

Direct Preference Optimization ([Rafailov et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)) trains on triples of a prompt $x$, a preferred response $y_w$ and a rejected one $y_l$. It starts from the same KL-constrained objective as RLHF and shows that the optimal policy can be fit directly with a single loss, with no reward model and no sampling:

$$\mathcal{L}_\text{DPO} = -\log \sigma\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_l \mid x)}\right)$$

$\pi_\text{ref}$ is a frozen copy of the starting model (normally your SFT checkpoint) and $\beta$ controls how far the policy may drift from it. With LoRA you don't need a second copy in memory: TRL computes the reference log-probs by disabling the adapter on the same base model.

```python
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer

# each line: {"prompt": ..., "chosen": ..., "rejected": ...}
dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files="preferences.jsonl", split="train")

trainer = DPOTrainer(
    model=sft_model,  # start from the SFT checkpoint, not the raw base
    args=DPOConfig(output_dir="dpo-out", beta=0.1, learning_rate=5e-6, num_train_epochs=1),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    processing_class=tokenizer,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
)
trainer.train()
```

DPO fits when it's easier to say "this answer is better than that one" than to write the ideal answer: tone, verbosity, refusing the right things, picking the better of two summaries. It is offline, though. The model only learns from the pairs you collected, and it can lower the likelihood of *both* responses as long as the margin grows, so watch the chosen-response log-probs during training, not only the loss.

### RLHF

The original recipe ([Ouyang et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)) has three stages: SFT, then a reward model trained on human rankings of sampled responses, then PPO, which samples fresh responses from the policy, scores them with the reward model, and updates the policy with a KL penalty that keeps it close to the SFT model. Because it samples on-policy, it can improve on prompts and failure modes that no preference pair covered. The price is four models in memory (policy, reference, reward, value), many more hyperparameters, and training runs that are notoriously unstable.

Most teams now reach for DPO first and keep online RL for cases where the reward can be computed rather than learned. That is the niche Bedrock's reinforcement fine-tuning targets. It uses GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300)), which drops PPO's value model by scoring each response against the other samples for the same prompt, and the reward comes from a verifiable grader (RLVR) or an LLM judge (RLAIF, the AI-feedback variant of RLHF) instead of a reward model trained on human labels.

### Picking one

- The model doesn't know your domain: continued pre-training, then SFT.
- You can write the ideal outputs: SFT.
- You can only rank outputs, not write them: DPO on top of SFT.
- You can score outputs automatically (tests pass, answer matches, schema validates): RL with GRPO, on Bedrock or with TRL's `GRPOTrainer`.

These stack in that order, and LoRA works at every stage.

## From a LoRA Adapter to Bedrock

If you trained the adapter yourself, [Custom Model Import](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html) is how it reaches Bedrock. It accepts Llama, Mistral, Qwen and a few other architectures as Hugging Face safetensors (fp16, bf16 or fp32), and it takes full weights, so the adapter has to be merged into the base first:

```python
merged = model.merge_and_unload()
merged.save_pretrained("llama3-8b-support", safe_serialization=True)
tokenizer.save_pretrained("llama3-8b-support")
# then: aws s3 sync llama3-8b-support s3://my-bucket/cmi/llama3-8b-support/

client = boto3.client("bedrock")
client.create_model_import_job(
    jobName="import-llama3-8b-support",
    importedModelName="llama3-8b-support",
    roleArn="arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/BedrockImportRole",
    modelDataSource={"s3DataSource": {"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/cmi/llama3-8b-support/"}},
)
```

Once the job completes, call the imported model's ARN through `bedrock-runtime` like any other model. The [merge section of the Llama 3 post](lora-finetuning-8b.qmd#merge-for-a-single-artifact) covers the merge step in more detail. The alternative is to skip local training and let Bedrock run it, which is what the rest of this post is about.

## AWS Bedrock Model Customization

Bedrock model customization exposes several workflows through one API, `CreateModelCustomizationJob`, selected by `customizationType`: `FINE_TUNING`, `CONTINUED_PRE_TRAINING`, `DISTILLATION` and, since December 2025, `REINFORCEMENT_FINE_TUNING`. This section covers RFT, SFT and distillation. Training data is read from S3 as `.jsonl`. The resulting custom model is stored by Bedrock in your account; your output S3 prefix only receives training metrics (and, for distillation, samples of the synthetic data).

### Reinforcement fine-tuning (new)

#### How it works

The model generates several candidate responses per prompt, a *reward function* scores each one, and Bedrock updates the model with GRPO to prefer higher-scoring responses (see [RLHF](#rlhf) above for how this differs from PPO). There's no gradient step against a single "correct" answer; the signal is relative quality across the sampled candidates. That suits tasks where correctness is graded rather than binary: multi-step reasoning, code generation, tool use, or open-ended writing where several answers are valid but some are clearly better.

Reward functions come in two flavors:

- RLVR (verifiable rewards): a rule-based grader for objective tasks (math, code execution, format checking).
- RLAIF (AI feedback): an LLM-as-judge grader for subjective tasks (instruction following, tone, RAG faithfulness). The console offers built-in judge prompt templates and turns them into a Lambda for you; through the API, both flavors are a `lambdaGrader`.

At launch (December 2025), RFT supports Amazon Nova 2 Lite in us-east-1.

#### Data format

Each record is an OpenAI-style chat-completion object with a `reference_answer` that the reward function grades against. It can be any structure your grader understands, not just text. A minimum of 100 records is required, and extra fields (e.g. `difficulty_level`, `domain`) are passed through to the grader as metadata:

```json
{
  "id": "algebra_001",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a math tutor"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Solve: 2x + 5 = 13"}
  ],
  "reference_answer": {"solution": "x = 4", "steps": ["2x = 8", "x = 4"]},
  "difficulty_level": "easy",
  "domain": "algebra"
}
```

#### Reward function (Lambda grader)

A custom grader receives the full conversation plus your `reference_answer` in `metadata`, and must return a normalized reward per sample. Raise the Lambda timeout above the 3-second default if your scoring runs code or calls a judge model:

```python
def lambda_handler(event, context):
    results = []
    for sample in event:
        response_text = sample["messages"][-1]["content"]
        reference = sample["metadata"]["reference_answer"]

        # your scoring logic: exact match, execution check, semantic diff, etc.
        score = score_response(response_text, reference)

        results.append({
            "id": sample["id"],
            "aggregate_reward_score": score,   # normalized, e.g. 0.0-1.0
            "metrics_list": [
                {"name": "accuracy", "value": score, "type": "Reward"}
            ],
        })
    return results
```

#### Launching a job (boto3)

```python
import boto3

client = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name="us-east-1")

response = client.create_model_customization_job(
    jobName="rft-math-tutor",
    customModelName="nova-lite-math-rft",
    roleArn="arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/BedrockCustomizationRole",
    baseModelIdentifier="amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0:256k",
    customizationType="REINFORCEMENT_FINE_TUNING",
    trainingDataConfig={"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/rft/train.jsonl"},
    validationDataConfig={"validators": [{"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/rft/val.jsonl"}]},
    outputDataConfig={"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/rft/output/"},
    customizationConfig={
        "rftConfig": {
            "graderConfig": {
                "lambdaGrader": {"lambdaArn": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:<account-id>:function:math-grader"}
            },
            "hyperParameters": {"epochCount": 3, "trainingSamplePerPrompt": 4},
        }
    },
)
```

#### Evaluation metrics

Training emits **average reward** and **validation reward** curves per checkpoint (validation reward normally trails training reward; if training reward climbs while validation reward falls, you're overfitting), plus **validation episode length** to track response verbosity. Beyond the training curves, Bedrock lets you A/B the RFT model against the base model with the same prompt set in the Playground, or run a full **Model Evaluation** job with your own test set for a systematic before/after comparison.

### Supervised fine-tuning

#### How it works

This is the SFT row of the table above, run on Bedrock's infrastructure. It's the right default when you already have good examples of the exact output you want.

#### Data format

For non-conversational tasks it's flat prompt/completion pairs:

```json
{"prompt": "Summarize the article about climate change.", "completion": "Climate change refers to the long-term alteration of temperature and typical weather patterns in a place."}
```

Chat formats differ by model family. Claude 3 Haiku takes a `system` string plus `messages`:

```json
{
  "system": "You are a helpful assistant.",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is AWS?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "It's Amazon Web Services."}
  ]
}
```

Converse-format models (Llama 3.2/3.3, Nova) need the `bedrock-conversation-2024` schema with content arrays instead, so check the [per-model data requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-prepare.html) before you build the file. Minimums also vary by model (32 records for Claude 3 Haiku, 100 for Llama 3.1/3.3), and the default cap is 10,000 training records, adjustable via service quota.

#### Launching a job (boto3)

Claude 3 Haiku fine-tuning runs in us-west-2, and it uses a learning-rate *multiplier* rather than an absolute learning rate:

```python
client = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name="us-west-2")

response = client.create_model_customization_job(
    jobName="sft-support-tone",
    customModelName="haiku-support-v1",
    roleArn="arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/BedrockCustomizationRole",
    baseModelIdentifier="anthropic.claude-3-haiku-20240307-v1:0:200k",
    customizationType="FINE_TUNING",
    trainingDataConfig={"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/sft/train.jsonl"},
    validationDataConfig={"validators": [{"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/sft/val.jsonl"}]},
    outputDataConfig={"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/sft/output/"},
    hyperParameters={"epochCount": "3", "batchSize": "8", "learningRateMultiplier": "1.0"},
)
```

#### Evaluation metrics

Bedrock writes **training and validation loss** curves to your output S3 prefix. They're useful for spotting under- or overfitting but say nothing about task quality. Pair them with a Bedrock **Model Evaluation** job on held-out prompts: its built-in accuracy metrics are **BERTScore** for summarization and **F1** for QA. Compute ROUGE yourself if you need it, and for open-ended output add an LLM-as-judge score and a manual side-by-side against the base model.

### Distillation

#### How it works

A large **teacher** model generates (or already has, via invocation logs) responses to your prompts, and those responses fine-tune a smaller, cheaper **student** model. Teacher and student must be one of the [pairs AWS supports](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prequisites-model-distillation.html), all within one model family (e.g. Nova Pro to Nova Lite, Llama 3.1 405B to Llama 3.1 8B); you can't distill across families. Bedrock can also apply its own data-synthesis techniques, such as paraphrasing prompts, to expand a small seed set to at most 15k prompt-response pairs before training the student. AWS claims distilled models are up to 500% faster and up to 75% cheaper, with less than 2% accuracy loss on use cases like RAG ([Bedrock Model Distillation](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/model-distillation/)).

#### Data format

The input is prompts only, in the `bedrock-conversation-2024` schema. Add an assistant turn to some records if you want to give the teacher golden examples:

```json
{"schemaVersion": "bedrock-conversation-2024", "system": [{"text": "You classify review sentiment."}], "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Classify the sentiment of this review: 'The battery life is incredible.'"}]}]}
```

Alternatively, reuse **invocation logs** already stored in S3 (with model invocation logging enabled), filtered by the `requestMetadata` you attached at invoke time:

```python
trainingDataConfig={
    "invocationLogsConfig": {
        "invocationLogSource": {"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/invocation-logs/"},
        "requestMetadataFilters": {"equals": {"project": "CustomerService"}},
        "usePromptResponse": True,
    }
}
```

With `usePromptResponse=True`, Bedrock trains on the logged responses instead of re-querying the teacher, so you pay no new teacher inference. This only works if the teacher in the job is the model that produced the logs.

#### Launching a job (boto3)

```python
client = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name="us-east-1")

response = client.create_model_customization_job(
    jobName="distill-support-classifier",
    customModelName="nova-lite-support-distilled",
    roleArn="arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/BedrockCustomizationRole",
    baseModelIdentifier="amazon.nova-lite-v1:0:300k",  # student model
    customizationType="DISTILLATION",
    trainingDataConfig={"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/distill/prompts.jsonl"},
    outputDataConfig={"s3Uri": "s3://my-bucket/distill/output/"},
    customizationConfig={
        "distillationConfig": {
            "teacherModelConfig": {"teacherModelIdentifier": "amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"}
        }
    },
)
```

#### Evaluation metrics

Because the whole point is a favorable accuracy/latency/cost trade, evaluate the student against the teacher on all three axes rather than accuracy alone: run a Bedrock **Model Evaluation** job with the same test prompts through both models to get a direct accuracy delta, then separately track p50/p90 **latency** and **cost per 1K tokens** for the student versus teacher to confirm the trade you're accepting is the one you intended.

### Serving the custom model

None of these jobs leaves you with something you can call yet. A customized model needs either Provisioned Throughput or an on-demand custom model deployment before `bedrock-runtime` will accept it, and that choice, not the training job, is usually where the bill grows. Check [the inference options for custom models](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-use.html) before you commit to a workflow.
